Thanks @siyuanfoundation and sorry I didn't have time to look at this until now.

Since the apply configuration types are client side APIs designed for a single client (controller or human) to construct an apply request, do we need to handle atomic vs. granular differently?  On the server side, we clearly need to handle the differences between atomic vs. granular to facilitate merging of change from multiple clients, but I'm a bit unclear on why a client would need to handle the construction of an applyconfiguration differently. Can you provide more detail on the use case that ran into problems to motivate this?
@dprotaso Can you provide more context about the use case regarding jpbetz's comments?

> Since the apply configuration types are client side APIs designed for a single client (controller or human) to construct an apply request, do we need to handle atomic vs. granular differently?

So this started with []byte. I don't think it really makes sense to append to the bytes rather than replacing them altogether. When I saw that, I realized it's not necessarily a property of being `[]byte` that it needs to be replaced altogether, it's probably a property of being atomic. I think it makes sense that atomic fields in general should be set all at once rather than in small parts.

issue_context.title: Generated ApplyConfiguration doesn't handle byte slices properly
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

`[]byte` slices aren't handled correctly in the generated apply configuration code

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/57144165f7afec3db71ca6f081ee8f4e4dfeab8a/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/applyconfigurations/admissionregistration/v1/webhookclientconfig.go#L54-L59

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected the byte slice to be assigned to the property

eg.

```go
// WithCABundle adds the given value to the CABundle field in the declarative configuration
// and returns the receiver, so that objects can be build by chaining "With" function invocations.
// If called multiple times, values provided by each call will be appended to the CABundle field.
func (b *WebhookClientConfigApplyConfiguration) WithCABundle(value []byte) *WebhookClientConfigApplyConfiguration {
	b.CABundle = value
	return b
}
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See code generator

comments: Yeah, the algorithm is that we append to lists, but I agree it doesn't make sense for a []byte. Hopefully `[]byte` are always treated as atomic. Actually, we should probably treat atomic lists differently from non-atomic (replace vs append).

review_comments:
I actually - don't think we should do a deep copy here. 

Most controllers will create these configs in a reconcile loop and this is excessive

Thanks for the feedback Dave, do you have concerns about performance specifically? what makes you think it's a problem? Do you think poeple will expect further changes to the values to match what they have in their config?

> do you have concerns about performance specifically?  what makes you think it's a problem? 

Our webhook CAs rarely change - and performing this copy for every reconcile where we are generating the apply config seems unnecesary.

I'm assuming the outgoing request doesn't mutate the byte array. 

> Do you think poeple will expect further changes to the values to match what they have in their config?

Can you clarify your question?

I'll agree that we probably don't need the copy:
1. caller can make the copy themselves if they want
2. the copy isn't deep anyway so the caller still needs to be aware and possibly properly copy.

Hi @dprotaso I have some different opinion on this. This PR is meant to fix the With function for all atomic slice types. Even though it is true that byte slices rarely change, we cannot work under the same assumption for other types of slices. I think we should use `copy` to be safer for more generic slice types. Although it is probably excessive for bytes, I think the performance impact is probably tiny if the byte length is not excessive.
Can we mark the non-new method deprecated (for atomic lists/maps) with a `// Deprecated: ...`?
